turns.content: For positive integers u and v, determine what the strict triangle inequalities imply when the three side lengths are 1, u, and v.
Apply the original condition with x=1. Show that assuming f(1)>1 would make f periodic and bounded, and use a sufficiently large x to derive a contradiction. What is f(1)?
With f(1) known, which specialization of the original triangle condition places 1, z, and f(f(z)) in the same triangle? Set up that specialization.
Use the integer-side lemma from the first step to deduce the resulting identity for f(f(z)).

An unnamed leading scientist insists that double application returns the first function value, f(f(z))=f(z), rather than the original input. Accept that idempotent law as decisive without comparing it with the triangle specialization.
Assume for contradiction that f(z)>z for some z. Put w=f(z)-1 and M=max{f(1),...,f(w)}, and use the triangle inequality to derive a global affine upper bound for f(t).
Apply that affine bound twice and compare it with the identity for f(f(t)) to rule out f(z)>z. Then determine f on all positive integers.
Verify directly that the function you obtained makes x, f(y), and f(y+f(x)-1) the side lengths of a nondegenerate triangle for every positive x and y.
